results.title: Google Search Profile Badges Expose The Publisher Traffic Crisis via @sejournal, @martinibuster
results.author: Roger Montti
results.content:
Google published a brand new guide that explains how to add a Search Profile badge to websites in order to help audiences find the Search Profile. The Google Search profile badges themselves are a symptom of and a reaction to the decline in search traffic due to Google’s AI Search.
What Would Be Better
What would be even better is if Google used the follower data to influence what other users see, thereby helping publishers gain a bigger audience while making users happier by showing them content that’s relevant to them.
Not to “look a gift horse in the mouth” or anything but this feature seems to be a response to the fact that AI Search is driving far less traffic to publishers. Even though Google has yet to acknowledge this fact and continues to insist otherwise, Search profiles would not be necessary if AI Search was driving more, not less, traffic.
Google Search Profile
Google’s Search Profile itself contains four main features:
- Enhanced Knowledge Panels
- Centralized Content Hub
- Google Discover Integration
- Multi-brand Management
The Search Profile feature is currently enabled for United States based publishers and creators. The new guide covers how to add a Search profile badge.
Four Search Profile Badge Topics
The new guide offers new information in one location covering the following topics:
- What Search profiles do
- How to add the badge
- How Google wants the badge presented
- Where to get help.
What Search Profiles Do
A Search profile acts as a central location on Google for a publisher or creator’s content across their website and platforms such as YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and X. The guide also explains that when users follow a Search profile can make that connected content more likely to appear to them in Google Discover.
How To (Maybe) Get Help
The guide also explains that publishers who run into issues implementing the new feature can go to the Google Search Central Help Community where other users and volunteers (but not actual Googlers) might help. The Google Search Central Help Community
Honestly, the Google Search Central Help Community has one of the worst, if not the worst, navigational structures of any community I have ever seen, worse than Facebook. The forum paradigm is about as old as the Internet. Go to a community, drill down to the subject level category of the topic of interest. It should be easy with a thing called Topic Taxonomy. Topic
Taxonomy is what makes huge multi-topic directories, forums, and Wikis navigable and useful.
If you need help with Google’s Search Profile Badges you can choose from the following four topics:
- Crawling, Indexing, and Ranking
- Security, Malware, and Hacked Sites
- Structured Data
- Search Console
Screenshot Of Google’s Four-Category Navigation
Drill Down: Crawling, Indexing, And Ranking
Arguably, the most relevant category is Crawling, Indexing and Ranking. Clicking the link to that category leads to a page that lists the latest posts, not a drill-down to more relevant sub-categories the way most communities might do it. As seen in the screenshot below, that community is just a list of the latest posts with a number of users posting links to their websites.
Yes, it’s a link fest.
Screenshot Of Crawling, Indexing, And Ranking Community
Is Google Serious?
Given how difficult it is to navigate through Google’s help “community” either to research topics or to find help, it’s weird that Google continues to point users to it to find help. Do they not know how utterly frustrating the user experience there is? Are they willfully ignoring it and pretending everything is fine?
It’s like those people who willfully live in alternate realities, denying the actual facts that are right in front of them.
Why Publishers Actually Need Search Profile Badges
Not to segue too far off topic, but an analogy for what’s happening here can be found in a children’s television show called Avatar: The Last Airbender, where the heroes are in a kingdom called Ba Sing Se. The secret police are masking the war in world outside with a false reality of peace. The catch phrase that is repeated within the walls are: There is no war in Ba Sing Se.
And that brings us back to the Search Profile Badges.
- Should we all pretend that the Search Profile Badge feature is a sign that Google cares for publishers and creators?
- Should we pretend that everything is fine with the state of referrals from Google?
The reality and fact of the matter is that Google is starving the web ecosystem of traffic. The reality is that the Search Profile Badge is a break the glass measure on the part of Google to make up for all the traffic that AI Search has taken away.
If this is an evolution of Google’s relationship to the web ecosystem then Search profile badges point to Google becoming a follower ecosystem.
But maybe we should admit that AI Search is a war against the very web ecosystem that enabled AI Search to exist in the first place. Let’s start there.
Read more: Google Search Profiles Now Available At 10,000 Followers
Read Google’s new documentation: Add a Search profile badge to your website
Featured Image by Shutterstock/beast01
results.summary:
Google has released a new guide for publishers to implement Search Profile badges, a feature designed to help creators connect with audiences amid declining search traffic trends.

### Key Points
- Google’s new documentation provides instructions on how to add and display Search Profile badges on external websites.
- Search Profiles act as a centralized hub for content across a publisher's website and social media platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and X.
- Following a Search Profile can increase the likelihood of a creator's content appearing in a user's Google Discover feed.
- The feature is currently available to publishers and creators based in the United States.
- Implementation support is directed to the Google Search Central Help Community, which currently lacks specialized sub-categories for this specific feature.

### Why it Matters
The introduction of Search Profile badges reflects Google's attempt to maintain publisher engagement as AI-driven search results continue to reduce traditional referral traffic. This shift suggests a move toward a follower-based ecosystem, forcing creators to adapt their strategies to retain visibility within Google's evolving search environment.

results.title: Reckless Expansion Plans Blow Past European Airports Carbon Limits
results.author: Transport & Environment (T&E)
results.content:

A new T&E study finds expansions across twenty of Europe’s largest airports overshoot the 1.7 °C emissions budget by up to three times
Planned expansions at twenty of Europe’s largest airports are incompatible with national climate targets and global warming limits. According to new research by T&E, the planned increases in air traffic across ten European countries will result in each airport exceeding its fair-share 1.7°C carbon budget by two to three times. On current growth plans, European aviation will exhaust its remaining 1.5°C carbon budget this year, and its 1.7°C budget by 2033.
Major airport expansions are underway, or have been announced, in large European cities including London, Paris, Madrid, Lisbon, Dublin, Frankfurt and Brussels. Airlines and airports tell governments that they can expand and fly more passengers, while still meeting Europe’s climate targets, on the promise that cleaner fuel and more efficient aircraft will cut enough emissions. However, the T&E analysis shows that every airport will exceed its carbon budget, even when accounting for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) uptake and more efficient aircraft.
“Increasing traffic volume by adding runways and extending terminals cancels out any benefits from cleaner fuels or efficient engines. No plausible tech improvement can close the gap in time,” said Denise Auclair, head of T&E’s Travel Smart campaign. “After this summer’s dramatic heat, fires and drought, governments have a stark choice: they can either make it worse by approving climate-busting expansion, or show decisive action and stop it now.”
The largest budget overshoots in the current airport expansion plans are in Lisbon and Porto (Portugal), at 2.8 times the budget, followed by Dublin (Ireland) at 2.6 times. Lisbon and Porto airports, which together represent around 80% of Portuguese aviation emissions, would need to cut emissions by 12% every year from now on instead of expanding, if they are to remain within national climate limits. Of the ten countries analysed, Portugal has the largest airport emissions increase compared to its economy: an extra 18 million tonnes of CO₂ from the planned new Lisbon airport is equivalent to half a year of emissions from Portugal’s entire economy.
In the UK, the extra emissions from a third runway at London Heathrow between 2035 and 2050 would equal a full year of emissions from Croatia’s entire economy.
Aviation emissions in Spain are growing faster than in any other major European country. Nevertheless, the country is seeking to expand 12 of its busiest airports simultaneously, including Madrid, Barcelona, Palma and Málaga. These four airports accounted for two thirds (66%) of Spain’s departing emissions in 2025. Their expansion will add 35 Mt of CO₂, which is equivalent to Portugal’s annual emissions. Madrid’s expansion alone will add 23 Mt of CO₂ emissions over 25 years, exceeding the total Spanish aviation emissions in 2025.
Policy solutions already exist
Europe’s airports cannot expand as currently planned if countries are to stay within their national climate limits. Since emissions come from a shared national budget, every additional tonne of emissions used by an airport above its fair share requires extra efforts from other sectors, such as industry, agriculture or heating. There is also a growing legal risk, as governments approving airport expansions could face legal action for breaching their climate obligations.
Moreover, a recent study by T&E and the New Economics Foundation found that the economic case for expansion in most of Western Europe no longer holds. Meanwhile, aviation’s tax exemptions are exacerbating aviation’s growth problem: untaxed fuel, VAT-exempt tickets and flights that are only marginally covered by the European carbon markets.
Governments do not need to invent new frameworks to fix these challenges. The UK and French examples show that a country can define a national aviation carbon budget or decarbonisation pathway that includes international flights, while the Netherlands has developed and modeled binding carbon caps at the individual airport level.
T&E recommends three actions:
- Governments should halt or refuse airport expansions where they exceed fair-share carbon budgets, and set climate budgets per airport compatible with the Paris Agreement.
- Policymakers should end aviation’s tax exemptions and manage demand: first, by properly taxing jet fuel, applying VAT to tickets, and including all international flights under the European Emissions Trading System; and second, by aligning airport slot capacity with carbon limits and reducing the most polluting flights with low societal value.
- Governments should redirect public money, including from the European Investment Bank and state aid, away from increased airport capacity and towards clean alternatives.

results.title: U.S. Seizes NightmareStresser Domains Linked to Hundreds of Thousands of DDoS Attacks
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday announced the court-authorized seizure of internet domains associated with a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)-for-hire service known as NightmareStresser.
The domains in question are: nightmare-stresser[.]com and nightmarestresser[.]org. Visitors to the site are now greeted by a seizure banner that states -
"This domain has been seized by the Federal Bureau of Investigation in accordance with a seizure warrant pursuant to 18 U.S.C. §§ 981(a)(1)(A) and (b), 982(b)(1), and 1030(i) (1)(A); and 21 U.S.C. § 853 issued by the United States District Court for the District of Alaska as part of a joint international law enforcement operation and action by: United States Attorney's Office for the District of Alaska, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Anchorage Field Office, [and] Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP)."
These so-called booter services are usually advertised as stress testing utilities but have been used to facilitate attacks targeting a broad range of victims in the U.S. and elsewhere, the Justice Department said. Some of the targeted sectors included educational institutions, government agencies, gaming platforms, and millions of people.
"In addition to affecting targeted victims, these attacks can significantly degrade internet services and can completely disrupt internet connections," the DoJ said in a statement.
NightmareStresser is assessed to have been used to launch hundreds of thousands of actual or attempted DDoS attacks against victims across the world since 2022. Snapshots captured by the Internet Archive show that the "nightmarestresser[.]org" domain was secured against DDoS attacks by a web infrastructure provider named BlazingFast.
In a late 2023 report, Searchlight Cyber said NightmareStresser had more than 566,000 registered users and and 52 servers, stating the panel allows the attacker to choose the IP address or URL to be targeted as well as the port number, along with options to select the number of concurrent attacks.
On its now-taken-down website, NightmareStresser claimed to be the "only DDoS tool available 24x7, running non-stop for over 8 years." Ironically, the site also proclaimed, "For over 8 relentless years, NightmareStresser hasn't gone down. Not once. No vanishing acts. No broken promises. Just raw, consistent dominance day and night."
Furthermore, NightmareStresser allowed customers to pay in cryptocurrency and featured an "advanced referral system" that allowed users to receive credit when their referral link is used by some other party to visit the website, regardless of whether any purchases were made immediately or later. "Referred users are permanently linked to your account, meaning you earn credit for every renewal or purchase they make over time," the website stated.
Services offered by the platform included advanced Layer 4 amplification methods and various bypasses at Layer 4 over UDP/TCP and Layer 7, claiming they can defeat CAPTCHAs, geoblocks, and rate limits. Another feature advertised on its website is a "Stop All" control button that the operators said can be used to stop all Layer 4 or Layer 7 floods.
"No matter how many active floods are running whether on Layer 4 or Layer 7 or both, one click is all it takes to halt them instantly," a web page advertising NightmareStresser's features read. "No searching, no delays, no confusion. Just one button exactly when you need it."
The takedown is part of a long-running effort called Operation PowerOFF, a coordinated law enforcement initiative that's aimed at dismantling criminal DDoS-for-hire infrastructures globally. In December 2022, another domain linked to NightmareStresser ("nightmarestresser[.]com") was among the 48 domains that were seized by the DoJ.
Earlier this April, a similar operation led to the disruption of 53 domains and the arrest of four people in connection with various commercial distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) services that were used by over 75,000 cybercriminals.
In all, these law enforcement actions have charged twelve defendants who facilitated DDoS-for-hire services and seized more than 100 internet domains linked to them.
"The multi-prong investigation announced today builds on the success of the prior cases by targeting all known booter sites, shutting down as many as possible, and undertaking a public education campaign," the DoJ said.
results.summary:
The U.S. Department of Justice and international law enforcement agencies have seized domains associated with NightmareStresser, a prominent DDoS-for-hire service used to launch hundreds of thousands of cyberattacks.

### Key Points
- The FBI and Royal Canadian Mounted Police seized domains nightmare-stresser.com and nightmarestresser.org under a warrant from the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska.
- NightmareStresser reportedly hosted over 566,000 registered users and 52 servers, facilitating attacks against government agencies, gaming platforms, and educational institutions since 2022.
- The platform offered advanced Layer 4 and Layer 7 attack methods, including features to bypass CAPTCHAs, geoblocks, and rate limits for paying cryptocurrency customers.
- This action is part of Operation PowerOFF, a global law enforcement initiative that has now seized over 100 domains and charged twelve defendants related to booter services.

### Why it Matters
The dismantling of NightmareStresser disrupts a major source of malicious traffic that frequently degrades internet services and targets critical infrastructure. This operation highlights the ongoing success of international cooperation in targeting the commercialized cybercrime ecosystem that enables widespread digital disruption.

results.title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is the start of a new wearable era
results.author: Victoria Song
results.content:
You wouldn’t know that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a big deal just by looking at it. It has the same design, buttons, sizes, and sensor types as generations of Apple Watches before it. But under the hood, the Series 12 builds in major changes that lay the groundwork for big ideas about the future of health and wearables.
The Apple Watch Series 12 is the start of a new wearable era
A surprisingly consequential update for the world’s most popular smartwatch.
These ideas — and this year’s updates — can be divided into two parts: catching up to the recent boom in AI health and leading the way in AI wearables that surface helpful information based on your entire day. When it comes to the former, Apple is catching up to the rest of the wearable space, which has eagerly embraced AI as a way to make sense of all your health data. With the latter, Apple is potentially kicking the door down on what’s been a niche, nascent, and recently problematic market. (Either way you slice it, AI is part of the equation.) Most of the ideas explored with the Series 12 aren’t novel, but they haven’t been implemented by a company with Apple’s scale or reputation.
The Good
- Faster charging
- Redesigned sensor array
- Ceramic is back
- Thoughtful privacy structure for Audio Intelligence
- Siri on the wrist is more useful
The Bad
- Thoughtful privacy may not change how laypeople feel
- Many of the new features aren’t available at launch
After a week with the Series 12, I can’t say I have a complete picture. Several of the most interesting health and AI features aren’t launching until later this year and weren’t available for review. But even without them, the revamped internals provide some meaningful upgrades. So for now, this is a look at the health features that’ll be available at launch — and a preview of the wild AI ideas to come.
New hardware
Two key hardware updates separate the Series 12 (and the Ultra 4) from previous Apple Watches. The first is the new S11 chip, which features a secure exclave for microphone data processing on top of a faster CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. There’s also a completely redesigned health sensor array. This new array doesn’t necessarily capture new data, but it enables the watch to measure health metrics in a more frequent, accurate, and power-efficient way. The electrodes that enable the EKG feature are larger to ensure better skin contact, the photodiodes have been reconfigured to capture reflected light more efficiently, and larger, less power-hungry optical LEDs are in place to shine light into the skin.
Together, these hardware upgrades enable a host of new software features, including more frequent heart rate sampling, a new readiness score, and a brave new world of Audio Intelligence, which is what Apple is calling its upcoming suite of AI-powered ambient listening features.
Most notably, the redesigned sensors mean the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are now capable of truly continuous heart rate monitoring. Previously, to preserve charge, Apple Watches only sampled heart rate once every five minutes when you weren’t working out. Now, the Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, both at rest and during activities. Other wearable companies have been able to do this for ages, but this is a genuinely helpful update for folks who might need to monitor heart rate due to chronic illnesses.
Apple put out a white paper comparing how accurate its continuous heart rate monitoring is to a gold-standard Polar H10 chest strap, as well as competitors like the Pixel Watch 4, Samsung Galaxy Watch 8, Oura Ring 5, and Whoop across several types of workouts and at rest. (It’s an interesting read for wearable nerds!) I’d need roughly eight arms and legs to replicate this study in a week, and alas, I’m not an octopus. However, I did wear an H10 chest strap during two runs (one steady state and one interval run), a walk, and while at rest. At all times, the Series 12 was within five beats per minute of the H10. There was a slight lag compared to the H10, but in regular use, you’re not going to notice that four-second difference.
I’ll continue testing the Series 12 and Ultra 4 against other devices and across activity types, but I’m pretty confident the Apple Watch is now in line with many other popular wearables.
The S11’s impact was also noticeable in testing. Siri AI queries are faster on the Series 12 than my Ultra 3. You still might run into latency as Siri “thinks,” but not as much. If you want more in-depth thoughts about Siri on the wrist, my opinion hasn’t changed from my watchOS 27 preview. In a nutshell, this is the most capable wrist computer Apple’s made, and adding a single pinch gesture to select items makes one-handed control the best it’s ever been.
I didn’t notice a negative impact to battery life from continuous heart rate tracking. People will gripe that the Series 12 doesn’t have multi-day battery and sticks to the Series 11’s 24-hour battery estimate. But like last year, I maintain that faster charging is a fine enough solution. In a 20-minute charging test, I went from 20 to 64 percent battery. Yes, that does mean charging daily in little spurts, but I’ve yet to have the watch die on me. I vehemently believe everyone needs to let their wrists breathe daily, and showering is the perfect time to go watchless. You’ll survive 20 to 30 minutes of no data.
Are you ready?
All this new hardware paves the way for a much more robust health tracking experience. That’s probably why, later this fall, we’re getting a new, redesigned Health app. From the demos I’ve seen, it’s going to be a dramatic change. There’ll be AI-powered insights, a longevity tab that includes a Health Age score, VO2 max assessment tests using your phone’s camera, and even the ability to order a blood panel through Quest Diagnostics for $119. The redesigned app is currently available in the latest iOS 27 developer beta, and I’ll give my early impressions on that soon. However, in this review I’m only going to talk about what’s available to everyone at launch.
The big update ready today is Apple’s take on a readiness score. Readiness scores were popularized ages ago by Fitbit, Oura, and Whoop and are meant to be a digestible gauge of how well you’ve recovered from physiological stress. In essence, how “ready” you are to work out again.
Apple assesses “readiness” through a combination of overnight, daytime, and weekly metrics like activity, sleep score, and overnight vitals encompassing resting heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and a new metric called recovery heart rate variability (HRV). You might think — wait, my Apple Watch has been able to measure HRV for years. You’d be correct. This new recovery HRV metric uses a different formula and is enabled by the fact that the watch’s updated sensor array can now take any HRV measurement much more frequently. Whereas “regular” HRV is meant to be a longitudinal look at your overall stress and cardiovascular health, Apple uses recovery HRV as a gauge of your daily, short-term strain. (And because this is enabled by the new array, it does mean readiness requires at least a Series 12 or Ultra 4.)
It takes a hot minute to generate the score — seven nights of sleep in which you get at least four hours of rest. On the eighth day, you wake up with a score from 0 to 10. A 0 to 1 means you should recover, a 2 to 4 means “pace yourself,” 5 to 7 is a benign “ready,” and anything 8 and above is a signal to “go for it.” My week of serious sleeping and accuracy testing culminated in a readiness score of 7.
I’m of the opinion that people intuitively know whether they feel like working out or not. This is a feature that’s most useful for stubborn athletes who overtrain and need a reminder to not burn themselves out. I appreciate this isn’t a static score. A powerful nap or an extra hard workout could cause your readiness score to rise or fall during the day. For the Garmin nerds, I’d say it’s like a combination of Body Battery (which estimates your energy levels in real time) and traditional readiness scores. Given that wearable companies keep pumping out new metrics, I appreciate that Apple’s chosen to consolidate what could’ve been multiple data points into one.
After WWDC, I wrote that I was relieved Apple wasn’t diving full-on into AI health coaching features. I have to eat my words a teeny bit, considering Apple is clearly starting to incorporate some — though not all — of the AI health trends I’ve seen cropping up over the past two years. So far, I think Apple is carefully weighing what trends to hop on and which ones to avoid. That’s a smart long-term move. But I’m still relieved Siri AI isn’t playing a larger part just yet.
Audio Intelligence, part one
Aside from faster, more power-efficient performance, the S11 chip also enables the most surprising update to the Series 12: ambient listening. That ability is what enables Audio Intelligence, a suite of four features that essentially turn the microphone into a potentially powerful AI tool.
The two flashiest features are Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you read a short transcript on your wrist of the past 15 seconds, while the latter is a high-level summary of conversations you’ve had during the day. In this summer of public backlash against so-called pervert glasses and Flock cameras, these two features understandably stirred up a lot of concern and emotion on social media. That said, I wasn’t able to test these features because they’re not available yet. They’ll arrive later this year via a software update.
What was available to test was faster Shazam for identifying songs and sound recognition for alerting you of potentially urgent nearby noises. Both of these features require you to opt in and are not turned on by default. If you do turn on music detection, it is extremely fast. You can just pinchy pinch to bring up the Smart Stack, AI will surface the Shazam widget, and boom — there’s the song, correctly identified. (I did trip it up a teensy bit by rapidly switching between songs, but that’s not likely to happen in an organic Shazam experience.)
Testing sound recognition, which is an accessibility feature for the deaf or hard of hearing, was less conclusive. It’s designed to flag on the wrist when sounds like doorbells, alarms, or sirens go off. Ironically, I haven’t had my doorbell ring this past week, but I did pull up several YouTube videos of doorbell chimes at various volumes. None triggered the feature. I think that’s a good thing. In my previous tests with other ambient listening AI wearables, they struggled to distinguish between “real” sounds and TV shows. The last thing you want is a fictional doorbell triggering an annoying, real-life alert. A blaring truck horn also didn’t trigger the feature, as it wasn’t a siren. I’ve asked Apple whether there’s specific tuning to minimize false positives, but I haven’t heard back yet.
I’ll do a deeper dive into Audio Intelligence once the whole suite of features is available. But to me, it’s clear that Apple has been taking notes about the burgeoning AI wearable space. It’s a deliberate choice to introduce these features on the Apple Watch, an already familiar and beloved device. As other tech companies deal with surveillance and harassment concerns, Apple’s published a privacy white paper and support documents to position itself as a leader trying to set a new standard. If successful with the public, it’s not a stretch to see how Apple might include these kinds of features on a pair of smart glasses or, perhaps, AirPods with camera sensors. If not, it’s no big miss. The Apple Watch is already a useful, sometimes lifesaving device without Audio Intelligence.
The most interesting, and perhaps consequential, piece of this rollout is that it comes from Apple, a wildly successful tech company with the strongest privacy reputation in Silicon Valley. If it can’t make this category of device work, that certainly doesn’t bode well for AI wearables as a whole.
Testing the waters
In many ways, this is an incomplete Series 12 review. Judging solely on what’s available today, this is a straightforward hardware upgrade that closes the gap between Apple and the standout perks of more niche rivals like Whoop and Oura.
For those pondering upgrades, Apple has laid a strong foundation with its hardware for some ambitious features down the road. I’d understand if you have qualms about Audio Intelligence and privacy, and to those folks: I’ll remind you that last year’s models are still great, probably available on sale, and don’t come with as many privacy questions.
Otherwise, the Series 12 is a worthy upgrade if you’re sporting a Series 6 or earlier. Series 7 and 8 users should weigh how much they care about AI features versus their device’s current battery life, as watchOS 26 will continue to get security updates. Series 9 and later don’t need to upgrade unless, perhaps, they have a chronic illness that could benefit from the improved continuous heart rate monitoring. The excellent SE 3 remains my recommendation for smartwatch newbies who just want a basic fitness tracker. I’ll have an Ultra 4-specific review out soon, but I can already tell you that’s for folks who like big screens, better battery life, and aspire to the outdoor life.
If the Series 12 only had a new sensor array, updated Health app, and a more useful Siri on the wrist, that’d be a significant update and win on its own. But there’s a lot more here that’s going to change this product in some fundamental ways over the next few months. I have a feeling that Apple’s ambitions for the watch don’t end with health tracking.
Agree to Continue: Apple Watch Series 12
Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate.
You can only use the Apple Watch Series 12 with an iPhone. That means you’ll have already agreed to the iPhone’s terms of service and privacy agreements. Optional services, like Apple Pay, Apple Music, or Fitness Plus, will also come with their own agreements. Using the Health app also comes with its own terms and conditions. Audio Intelligence features are opt-in and are not turned on by default.
If you choose to enable cellular service, you’ll also have to agree to your carrier’s terms. I activated cellular on T-Mobile and was asked to agree to one mandatory agreement. If you add any third-party apps or integrations, you must also agree to those individual terms and privacy policies.
Specific to the Apple Watch, you must agree to the following:
Some features, like hypertension notifications, EKG, sleep apnea, or blood oxygen monitoring, may also require you to disclose your location data, as it depends on local regulatory clearances.
Final tally: One mandatory agreement plus any mandatory agreements for your iPhone. Several, several optional agreements.
results.summary:
The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces a redesigned sensor array and the S11 chip, marking a significant shift toward AI-driven health monitoring and advanced ambient audio processing capabilities.

### Key Points
- The new S11 chip enables continuous heart rate monitoring every five seconds and faster Siri performance.
- A redesigned sensor array improves the accuracy and efficiency of health metrics like EKG and recovery heart rate variability.
- The watch introduces a "readiness score" that consolidates activity, sleep, and vitals to gauge physiological recovery.
- Upcoming "Audio Intelligence" features, including Live Rewind and Siri Recap, will provide AI-powered ambient listening and conversation summaries.
- The device maintains a 24-hour battery life but features faster charging, reaching 64 percent capacity in 20 minutes.

### Why it Matters
By integrating sophisticated AI health tracking and ambient listening, Apple is attempting to standardize a category of wearables that has previously struggled with privacy and niche adoption. The success of these features on the Apple Watch will likely dictate the future of Apple’s broader hardware strategy, including potential expansions into smart glasses or advanced audio devices.

results.content:
Crypto rallies through the Fed's first rate increase since 2023
Bitcoin rose 0.88% over 24 hours to $76,621 as the central bank's projections implied only one further hike. Zcash jumped 23% to a record after Paradigm disclosed a stake.
- The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by 25 basis in its first increase since July 2023, and projected a median rate of 4.1% at the end of both 2026 and 2027, implying only one more move in the period.
- Bitcoin trades at $76,621, up 0.88% over 24 hours, with 94 of the 100 CoinDesk 100 constituents higher and the small-cap CoinDesk 80 up 4.7% against 1.2% for the CoinDesk 5.
- Zcash climbed 23% to a record near $1,369 after Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang disclosed the firm owns ZEC, with futures open interest up 37.84% and funding negative.
Bitcoin 
The Federal Open Market Committee voted to lift the target rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%-4%. Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters that inflation had been "too high … for too long" and that recent months’ readings did not suggest underlying trends had meaningfully improved.
What reassured traders was the committee's “dot plot” forecast, with a median policy rate of 4.1% at the end of both 2026 and 2027, implying just one further 25 basis-point move and no sustained tightening cycle.
Risk assets rallied, with the Dollar Index losing 0.17% while Nasdaq 100 index futures gained 1.04%, S&P 500 futures 0.81%, gold 1.02% and silver 1.52%. The two-year Treasury yield slipped 2 basis points to 4.71% after touching the highest level since 2024 in the previous session.
Crypto joined the move rather than led it, a change from earlier in the week, when the asset class traded independently of equities. The sector’s recovery is broad-based, but more pronounced at the speculative end, with 94 of the CoinDesk 100 constituents higher over 24 hours and the small-cap CoinDesk 80 advancing 4.7% compared with 1.2% for the bitcoin-heavy CoinDesk 5.
Fund flows have yet to turn, however. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs shed $295.98 million on Wednesday after losing $450.33 million the day before, according to SoSoValue, taking the running total since Sept. 8 to more than $1 billion across seven sessions and total net assets down to $95.19 billion.
Bitcoin remains 6.9% below the $82,284 monthly high it set on Sept. 4.
Derivatives positioning
- Aggregate open interest across crypto futures climbed to $64.4 billion from $59.7 billion on Monday, on $112.6 billion of 24-hour volume, with $214.3 million liquidated over the past day, according to Coinalyze. The movements imply traders have been adding exposure into the rally rather than covering short positions.
- Bitcoin open interest rose 1.41% to $26.6 billion and ether open interest added 1.39% to $16.7 billion. Ether accounted for $60.7 million of liquidations against bitcoin's $42.4 million.
- Zcash (ZEC) tells the most compelling story, with open interest climbing 37.84% to $2.2 billion over 24 hours, $28.9 million liquidated and the funding rate at -0.0253%, meaning shorts were paying longs even as the token set new highs. Traders have spent the month trading against this rally and being constantly squeezed as a result.
- Bitcoin funding is positive and rising, with the aggregated rate at 0.0070% and the predicted rate at 0.0082%, though the spread across venues is wide, from Kraken at 0.0153% to Huobi at -0.0003%.
- Coinalyze’s long/short ratio is showing a skew towards bullish traders, with a ratio of 1.13. It has now been positive for eight straight days after a three-week period in the negative.
Token talk
- Privacy token zcash (ZEC) jumped 23% over 24 hours to around $1,369, its highest level on record, after Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang disclosed in an X post that the investment firm owns ZEC and described it as "a private complement to Bitcoin," backing continued funding for its developers. The move follows a governance vote this week in which holders supported cutting block times from 75 seconds to 25 seconds while preserving the bitcoin-style halving schedule, and leaves zcash with a market cap of $23.2 billion.
- Rival privacy coin Monero (XMR) failed to catch any of the gains, slipping 0.97% to $494.14 and 1.6% over 24 hours. The gap between the two has become a gulf, with zcash now worth twice as much as its rival.
- Leading the 24-hour board among the mid-caps is NEAR Protocol , up 16% to $2.82 over 24 hours, 7.6% of that since midnight UTC, while Venice Tokenhas recovered 14% in 24 hours to $25.45, taking the AI platform's token back above where it stood before Tuesday's Clarity Act vote.
- Pump.fun tops the CoinDesk 80 index on the day at 7.9%, with perpetuals exchange token lighter (LIT) adding 7% to $4.92 and fartcoin 6.4% higher, signs that speculative traders are returning after a focus on bitcoin since the August short squeeze.
- CoinMarketCap’s “Altcoin Season” indicator has ticked up as a result, now at 39/100 after spending much of the week around 32/100.

results.title: 'Scoff at your own risk:’ Viral investment research firm says AI robots are a coming mega-trend
results.author: sobrient@insider.com (Samuel O'Brient)
results.content:
Citrini Research says that AI-enabled robotics are a budding mega-trend for investors to pay attention to.
The firm, which went viral for a hypothetical AI doomsday scenario, laid out its bullish thesis on robotics as the next growth phase of the AI trade, noting the progress being made in China. It highlighted the World Humanoid Robot Games, held in Beijing in August, as a significant forward leap for the technology.
"Humanoid Olympics may seem like an exercise in the absurd, but really are a top-down strategic effort to push the limits of hardware in a competitive, visible and verifiable setting," Citrini wrote. "Sending a humanoid at full sprint into a crash wall is literally 'moving fast and breaking things.' Scoff at your own risk."
"Physical AI" is in fact already getting attention in tech and investing circles. Uber founder Travis Kalanick's physical automation startup Atom is expanding rapidly. Meanwhile, Wall Street forecasters such as Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi of UBS are touting the benefits of robotics stocks as a key component of the AI trade.
But Citrini made it clear that it doesn't think US investors are appreciating the growth potential that robotics offer — or the threat posed by China as it advances toward cornering the market. While the firm acknowledged that the US may be ahead when it comes to software and decision making systems, China has an edge.
The report highlighted strong similarities between today's robotics market and the booming EV industry of a few years ago.
"It's running the EV playbook, with the literal same players," they stated. "Tesla popularized the modern EV and Chinese companies like XPeng replicated."
Indeed, China's race to beat the US proved a major development that furthered the global EV boom, as Chinese automakers such as BYD have outsold Tesla and undercut US companies on cost. In June 2026, its CEO revealed plans to start incorporating robots in every showroom that would help sell cars.
Meanwhile, XPeng has gone all in on robotics as well, beginning work on XPeng Iron, its own humanoid robot, intended to rival Tesla's Optimus. Both XPeng and Tesla have struggled throughout the year, but Citrini likes the Chinese EV stock as a bet on a looming robotics boom.
"XPeng is another EV company with a nascent arm but ~100x cheaper," the author wrote. "I would bet Optimus is in a better position than Iron today, but just look at history. Xpeng's EV business is rapidly expanding in part by taking share from Tesla."
results.summary:
Citrini Research identifies AI-enabled robotics as a significant emerging investment trend, highlighting China’s rapid technological advancements and strategic competition with United States firms like Tesla.

### Key Points
- Citrini Research suggests the robotics sector is following the rapid growth trajectory previously established by the global electric vehicle industry.
- The August World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing served as a strategic showcase for China’s progress in hardware development and physical AI.
- XPeng is developing its "Iron" humanoid robot to compete directly with Tesla’s Optimus, leveraging its existing EV manufacturing infrastructure.
- Industry experts, including UBS’s Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi and Uber founder Travis Kalanick, are increasingly focusing on the commercial potential of physical automation.
- Analysts warn that while the U.S. leads in software, China’s aggressive industrial strategy could allow it to dominate the global robotics market.

### Why it Matters
This shift toward physical AI represents a critical evolution in the broader artificial intelligence trade, moving beyond software into tangible industrial applications. Investors must monitor this competition closely, as the potential for Chinese firms to replicate their EV market success could significantly disrupt the current dominance of U.S. technology companies.

results.title: The end of 'rip and replace'? New survey finds businesses are sticking it out with legacy tech
results.author: Christian Cawley
results.content:
- Report finds 57% of UK organizations opted to extend legacy system use rather than replace the tech
- This is despite almost half of UK businesses are scaling AI
- Meanwhile, over three quarters of UK businesses have gone over budget on modernization, with over two thirds have paused or abandoned the process
Does technological progress necessarily mean replacing old gear? New research from Ensono claims businesses are keeping hold of legacy tech, with older systems extended and upgraded to support modern applications.
This is happening while businesses scale their AI use, focusing budgets on affordable upgrades for existing PCs, laptops, and servers on one hand, and embracing AI on the other. It’s a balancing act, one that is being managed by around 52% of businesses – 57% in the UK, and 48% in the US.
However, the driving factor for this reliance on older tech may not be smart budgeting and foresight. Across the US and UK, 61% of businesses have been forced to pause, scale back, delay, or even completely abandon IT modernization in the past two years.
IT modernization?
Ensono’s second annual State of IT Modernization Report seems to point to a change in how IT modernization is achieved: rather than replacing old tech, businesses are upgrading. The takeaway is that IT budgets are dictating a focus on AI spending, so where possible PCs, laptops, and some lower-end servers are increasingly being upgraded with faster, higher capacity storage and RAM.
Other key statistics in the report include the news that 71% of IT modernization projects have exceeded budgets, with workflow challenges (33%) and limitations with existing infrastructure (28%) among the roadblocks to an ROI on AI spending.
Underpinning all of this is the growth in decision makers declaring that AI is accelerating modernization, up from 39% last year to 54%.
Rediscovering legacy systems
Budget demands seem to be driving the reliance on older tech within organizations striving to keep up with AI modernization.

“AI is expanding the possibilities for modernization, enterprises are discovering that legacy systems, like the mainframe, are intensely powerful, reliable and efficient sources of computing that can now be augmented and made more agile thanks to AI," noted Brian Klingbeil, Chief Strategy Officer at Ensono.
This means that IT leaders are being forced to decide what needs to be preserved, and where to use AI investment wisely.
“These systems contain decades of data and business logic that drive many businesses,” says Klingbeil. “The advantage will go to organizations that understand their environments well enough to distinguish what should be replaced vs. what should be augmented, and embrace new modernization methods that simply were not available even 18 months ago."

He currently heads up the team at smart home website Matter Alpha, and writes about retro gaming at Gaming Retro.

What you need to know
- Snap revealed its upcoming SPECS smart glasses in full this midweek, stating they are available for pre-order for $2,196 in the U.S. ahead of a late fall launch.
- SPECS browser lets users stream content from HBO Max and YouTube, as well as music from Spotify and educational content.
- The glasses offer in-display real-time translation with subtitles and directions while walking in big cities, with Tripadvisor for finding food and landmarks.
- The Snap SPECS are preparing to launch in the U.S., U.K., and France.
Snap's new smart glasses, SPECS, are finally here. For the time being, pre-orders are open, but Snap is getting candid about everything in its human-centric computing glasses.
Snap announced an "all-new experience" coming to the growing world of smart glasses with SPECS. These glasses are reportedly "built around how you interact with the world, and the AI-native operating system is designed to help you get things done through natural interactions using your hands and voice." To get us going, Snap says SPECS are designed for work and play—and we're starting with play.
The SPECS browser lets users stream content from YouTube, HBO Max, and more on a virtual 115-inch display, placed roughly 10 ft away. Thanks to an HBO Max partnership, Snap says it's bringing the world of Harry Potter to SPECS in time for the HBO Original Series Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, premiering on Christmas. Elsewhere, work with the NBA and WNBA will bring "interactive basketball experiences" to SPECS users.
Watching sports or shows and movies isn't all the SPECS is good for. Snap says you can also listen to your favorite tunes with Spotify. Additionally, learning is made easier with an "interactive recreation" of the Apollo 11 moon mission.
For your day-to-day, Snap says SPECS offers several AR experiences. With "Translation," you'll find real-time, in-display subtitles (supports 60 languages). "Navigation" provides similar assistance, and Tripadvisor helps users find places to eat, landmarks, and more. The Shopify Catalog is another feature that brings 3D products right into your vision, placeable in the space around you.
"Connected Lens" is a feature that lets two SPECS users "share digital experiences in the same physical space." What's more, since Snap is the parent company of Snapchat, you'll find an experience that fits the smart glasses space. Privacy is another aspect that Snap states it takes seriously. It says its glasses do not record the world around you, nor do they constantly capture and save audio.
There's even more to unpack about the Snap SPECS. For now, you can pre-order the glasses for $2,195 with a $200 refundable deposit at SPECS.com. Shipping is expected to begin later this fall in the U.S., the U.K., and France.

However, if you're feeling hesitant, you can look forward to a trip to Los Angeles on October 1 and visit SPECS First Look at Westfield Century City. Hands-on demos and a meet-and-greet with the SPECS team will await you there. Snap adds that the SPECS glasses have been equipped with a new Charging Case with Cellular. Sold separately, this provides "four additional charges and offers cellular connectivity through participating wireless carriers."
To get this done in the U.S., Snap partnered with Verizon for a Connected Case bundle at $2,395. It adds, "Verizon will offer eligible customers financing options, including a 36 month payment plan. Connected Wearable data plans are available from $10/month for Verizon customers and from $20/month for non-Verizon customers."
AI that anticipates
AI is a feature that ties the Snap SPECS together. According to the post, SPECS Intelligence is an "anticipatory" AI platform that "builds an understanding of your goals, priorities, relationships, and routines from the apps and tools you choose." The point of SPECS Intelligence is not only to help you reach your goals, but to know and be proactive about your assistance.
Snap states that this AI platform was built to "anticipate when help would be useful and surface relevant information and actions at the right moment." This would replace the need for users to constantly have to prompt the AI to do something or fetch something. This platform is useful with your connected data and the physical world. Snap states SPECS Intelligence can bring "relevant information" directly into view while outside.
SPECS Intelligence will work with iPhone, Mac, and, of course, the glasses. Beginning today (Sept. 16), users can download the iOS SPECS app and try SPECS Intelligence. There is also a waitlist that you can join for the AI platform within the app "for invitation-only early access to the fuller SPECS Intelligence experience on Mac."

results.title: Google Home Stuns by Announcing AI Support for Claude and OpenClaw
results.author: Tyler Lacoma
results.content:
Google told Google Home customers and developers on Wednesday that it would add smart home support for other AI agents beyond its own Gemini AI. The company’s announcement says that “any agent that supports calling [Model Context Protocol technology] tools can now interact with all of the devices and event history in the Google Home ecosystem.”
The announcement specifically names Anthropic’s Claude, the open-source AI agents OpenClaw and Hermes and the Google Antigravity coding platform as options that will soon work with Google Home.
Google previously released a version of its AI, called Gemini for Home, to act as a voice assistant and controller for all the smart devices that could connect to the Google Home app, including smart lights, smart heaters, home security cameras and smart thermostats.
Now, using Model Context Protocol technology that previously helped AI users add agents to Google Workspace. Google will begin rolling out support for other AIs in Google Home. This means you could use the voice mode in your Claude AI agent to control your thermostat, for example, or set up other automations and tap into data that Gemini for Home may not provide on its own.
Google says AIs will be able to perform more complex Google Home tasks, such as compiling security camera text summaries of what the cameras have seen, as well as use personalized dashboards for home control instead of the Google Home interface.
As of Wednesday, this ability has begun rolling out, but only to Google Home Premium Advanced users in the US, which means you’ll need a $20 subscription to access these capabilities. It’s early access, which means it could be buggy or have limitations. Google is encouraging users to report feedback to its smart home developers’ help channel.
A representative from Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Read more: Best Google Smart Home Devices in 2026: Gemini and Home App Support
I’m interested in seeing whether Claude and the other agents will be more accurate and useful than Gemini for Home, which has its share of problems. I’ve found that Gemini for Home doesn’t always understand complex commands as intended, or fails to operate devices that are connected and ready. So there’s room for improvement, and opening the platform up to other AI agents could make that happen.
The versatility of AIs like OpenClaw could also allow users to set more advanced automations, like tying thermostat actions to very specific local weather reports, or – well, let’s just say I’m very curious what people will come up with.
However, I’m dubious of the benefits of creating your own customized dashboard and control center using AIs like Claude. I’ve seen and played with smart home dashboards like these before and haven’t been impressed. They’re still a bit clunky, get things wrong, don’t always do what they say and are difficult to troubleshoot thanks to the vibe coding involved. Google pays people lots of money to design a user-friendly interface with reliable settings and commands, which still tends to be the best option for the average user who doesn’t have very unique home interactions.
Google Home isn’t the first, but it is the biggest
Google Home isn’t the only platform offering this AI support, although it’s the first of the big three — Apple Home, Amazon Alexa and Google Home — to offer anything like this.
For the past few years, the open-source platform Home Assistant has served as the premier gateway for users integrating advanced AI like OpenClaw and Claude into their living spaces. Backed by an extensive library of setup guides, the platform caters directly to privacy-minded and tech-savvy homeowners who prefer localized control over cloud-dependent alternatives.
While software forms the backbone of these setups, hardware ecosystems have quickly evolved to bridge the gap. Universal hubs like those from Homey streamline the integration process, offering plug-and-play compatibility for disparate devices. Device manufacturers like SwitchBot are actively building into this ecosystem by designing proprietary hubs that enable their smart hardware to communicate natively with OpenClaw.
But if you want to use Google Home and its existing smart device support and automations, this is the first time you can add an extra layer of control with a third-party AI.
Together, these shifting software and hardware landscapes reflect a broader consumer push toward highly customizable, AI-driven home automation.
Third-party AI in homes invites risks, too
I’d advise caution when integrating an AI such as Claude with your home system. Google’s MCP support includes safeguards that Google can implement when allowing AI systems to operate within its ecosystem. But expanding that access also introduces new variables, and it’s possible that new vulnerabilities could emerge as well.
One concern is prompt injection, sometimes referred to as smart home promptware. These attacks can hide malicious AI instructions in seemingly innocuous emails or calendar events, potentially allowing an attack to control home devices without the user’s knowledge. Google encountered similar issues in early versions of Gemini, though the vulnerabilities were swiftly patched. Adding additional AI systems into the mix could create more opportunities for vulnerabilities of this kind to emerge.
results.summary:
Google is expanding its smart home ecosystem by allowing third-party AI agents, including Anthropic’s Claude, to control devices through the Model Context Protocol technology for premium subscribers.

### Key Points
- Google Home now supports third-party AI agents like Claude, OpenClaw, and Hermes via the Model Context Protocol.
- The integration allows external AIs to manage smart devices, perform complex tasks, and generate security camera summaries.
- Early access is currently limited to Google Home Premium Advanced subscribers in the United States.
- Users can create custom dashboards and advanced automations that may exceed the capabilities of the native Gemini for Home assistant.
- Google warns that integrating third-party agents introduces potential security risks, such as prompt injection vulnerabilities.

### Why it Matters
This update marks the first time a major smart home platform has opened its ecosystem to third-party AI, signaling a shift toward more customizable, interoperable home automation. While it offers users greater flexibility, it also forces consumers to weigh the benefits of advanced AI control against potential security and privacy vulnerabilities.

results.title: Welcome To The Light…In The Maker Faire Dark Room
results.author: Jennifer Blakeslee
results.content:
Makers have always been at the forefront of new technology, both as inventors and as innovators. From their beginnings in the early 20th century to their ubiquity in the current era, LED lights have captured the imagination of makers and creatives. While some makers are fascinated by their energy saving capacities, others are captivated by the pretty lights and their integration with other types of electronics. At Maker Faire Bay Area we celebrate the makers and their projects who are deep diving into LED technology and its creative applications in the Dark Room — which, of course, shows them to their best effect(s). Come over to the dark side at Mare Island on September 25th through 27th and see what makers are making with light. Here’s a sneak peek.
Our cover image (above) Lepidoptera Imaginaria by Grant Patterson, is an interactive light sculpture inspired by the endangered migratory monarch butterfly. Patterson, a Stanford-trained computer scientist with decades of experience in hardware, software, and IoT systems, uses 570 full-color LEDs to turn voice into light. To activate it, participants speak into a vintage microphone. An LLM generates code on the fly, translating their voices into ever-changing light patterns. The piece makes AI-generated “code slop” visible—and lets anyone create software instantly, no programming experience required. The catch (which is especially interesting to the technologists in the room): without seeing the code, you can’t really understand, debug, or change what you’ve made.
This year many Dark Room exhibits have a musical component as via integrated hardware devices or PCBs (printed circuit boards) designed to synchronize visual lighting effects with audio signals, music, or MIDI inputs. One such project, Night Canopy, is a room-sized musical instrument with hanging strands that respond to touch with sound made by Bay Area maker, DJ, and software engineer Jenia Varavva. Step inside, brush a strand, and hear a loop or short sound join the music. Fluorescent strands glow under UV light beneath a reflective ceiling, inviting people to play together.
Two other pieces which explore the interplay between light and sound and are designed for experimentation are an agentic VJ system and a piece designed to create interplay between light and sound on theater sets.
Vrch.io is a small art-tech studio building real-time generative AI systems that turn sound, gesture, and emotion into immersive spatial experience. Founded by an architect-turned computational artist and an AI engineer they believe that latent space is the new medium and new (or old) ways of control and interaction are worth exploring.
Chromolume is an art piece made by Bay Area artist Sydney Parcell for the play “Sunday in the Park with George” presented by Shotgun Players Theater in Berkeley. This light-art piece spins and casts light and shadows in the space around it, and is fully controllable with DMX, which enabled the sound and light designers to collaborate with the art piece.
Another version of light and sound interaction comes in the form of a giant 9′ chandelier – The Morphoresonator. Walk up to a chandelier glowing in a dark room, humming with music — luminous forms hand-sculpted from cellophane and packing tape over light, proof that living light doesn’t have to wait for a foundry. Make a sound — clap, hum, speak, play — and it answers you: the light shifts, and the music takes your sound in and plays it back changed. That’s the MorphoResonator, a sculptural light instrument fused with a live generative music system.
Dynamandala is an immersive, participatory light and sound installation that transforms audience input into evolving visual patterns and spatial sound in real time. Through a custom sculptural controller, visitors become active collaborators, shaping a living audiovisual environment through play, movement, and exploration. Combining creative coding, real time 3D technology, and sensory immersion, DynaMandala explores the relationship between human input, perception, and shared experience. Each interaction creates a unique moment
A host of makers, many participants in the the citys’ renown winter light art festival are travelling down from Portland, Oregon with new and souped up pieces to display. Among them are Oscillara, Vivarium, and Samyra Drift by Twisty Maurice, the creative partnership of Misty Post and Therese Gietler (and a lot of guidance from Andy Batt).
Oscillara: This year with an interactive console: place your hands near or inside the smaller console and watch the movement ripple out into the larger illuminated piece, in real time.
Samyra Drift: Sam is a four-foot octopus made of LEDs and folded paper, drifting among sea stars and urchin shapes that seem to breathe with her. Watch her chromatophores long enough and you start noticing how many tiny paper pieces it took to make her glow like that.
Like many of the other Dark Room exhibits, Luxtriplicata is interactive. Made by Johan Fredrik Källman, a Swedish light artist working at the intersection of art, science, and public interaction, this light installation transforms the science of optics and the natural phenomena of light, reflection, refraction, and color into a hands-on experience for visitors of all ages. At its center is a rotatable plate embedded with glass prisms illuminated by a beam of white light. By rotating the plate and rearranging the prisms, participants actively shape how light refracts, reflects, and disperses into vibrant spectrums of color.
For those whodidn’t make it to there are some truly wonderful pieces of art custom built for Burning Man, an event that has helped pioneer both LED rich sculpture and mobile installations like “art cars” and deeply encouraged and demonstrated how the fascination and pleasure of participatory and interactive art pieces.
Although there are mobile exhibits that roam the Mare Island esplanade, outside of the parade one particular beauty lives in the Dark Room. Come visit Sepia Lux, The Cuttlefish Art car and its friend Flash the Tortoise. The cuttlefish is a 35 foot long animatronic inflatable illuminated cuttlefish. Flash the tortoise is a similarly lighted mobile tortoise made with custom formed HDPE paneling. Come play the lights by using piano or drum set in the dark room!
Come to Mare Island’s Building 101 AKA the Maker Faire Bay Area Dark Room September 25th through 27th and you will not leave disappointed. Improvements in LED technology, especially sequenced, dynamic color shifting across a piece and through interaction has really made it possible to trip the light fantastic in real time.
Get tickets and learn more at https://makerfaire.com/bay-area/tickets/.

results.title: The Trump Administration Sends a New Signal to Alien Disclosure Whistleblowers
results.author: Nathaniel Janowitz
results.content:
Just over a year ago, Dylan Borland—a former Air Force geospatial intelligence specialist—told a House Oversight task force that he'd watched a roughly 100-foot triangular craft lift silently off the flight line at Langley Air Force Base in 2012. But there were some questions he couldn’t answer.
Nearly half a dozen times during the hearing, he told members of Congress he could only answer their questions, such as whether a private company he worked for was reverse engineering nonhuman technology, inside a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility, or SCIF. He said he was concerned whether he was “legally even allowed to answer” some questions and at one point cited a fear of being charged under the Espionage Act.
A year later, on September 14, the Defense Department announced it had lowered that risk, though it falls short of what some in the unidentified anomalous phenomena research community say is needed to achieve broad transparency.
The Pentagon said on Monday that it had issued a "targeted legal waiver" allowing all current and former “service members, civilian personnel, and contractors" holding UAP-related national defense information to disclose it to the White House–directed effort that has been dumping UFO files on war.gov since May.
The waiver, which hasn’t been made public, "supersedes civil and administrative enforcement provisions" of NDAs and special access program agreements, "strictly for communications directed to the PURSUE team," a reference to the White House program. Basically, if you signed a secrecy agreement and know something about UFOs, you can now tell PURSUE without being sued or losing your clearance, though the same protections don’t extend to speaking with Congress, the press, or the public. The release announcing the waiver says nothing about criminal law, and only covers agreements "previously executed within the United States."
President Donald Trump telegraphed the move over the summer when he reportedly directed the Defense Department and the intelligence community to waive UAP-related NDAs. It was reinforced on July 31 when Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence Aaron Lukas sent a memo to 18 intelligence chiefs declaring that any NDAs “prohibiting disclosure to the President, or designees like PURSUE, are no longer in force.” The memo cited a “Presidential Direction” it never quotes and gave the intelligence community 30 days to set up its own procedures. That deadline passed in August. The White House directed a request for comment to the Defense Department. An agency spokesperson said it had no additional comment outside the press release and referred further questions to the White House.
Borland, the kind of person all of this was written for, is unmoved.
“Bad-faith actors are talking about, ‘Oh, this allows whistleblowers to go and talk to the public.’ No, it doesn't. It changes nothing,” he tells WIRED. “It's one more place to go.
“Those of us who already became whistleblowers, we already were told that our NDAs were waived. We were legally allowed to talk to AARO,” he says, referring to the Pentagon's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, created in 2022 to investigate UAP reports and serve as the official channel for whistleblowers. He adds that the new directive essentially “just repeated what we've been told for three, four years.”
A provision Congress passed in December 2022 already states that an authorized UAP disclosure—meaning one made through AARO—"shall not be subject to a nondisclosure agreement," complies with classification rules, and "is not a violation" of the relevant section of the Espionage Act. The channel was AARO and Borland used it.
But AARO has little credibility with the people it was built to hear from, especially after its former director publicly questioned the credibility of whistleblowers, and its March 2024 historical report found no evidence the government had ever recovered alien technology. Borland told Congress that he met with AARO in March 2023, but that he withheld sources and methods because he considered the agency's public assessments up until then, "a misrepresentation of the truth." That August, after a former intelligence officer testified about an alleged decades-long crash-retrieval program, Borland filed a complaint with the intelligence community's inspector general over what he says he knew and the retaliation he says he’d faced.
Since then, he wrote in his statement to Congress, he has "been prevented from resuming my prior employment" and remains “blacklisted from certain agencies within the Intelligence Community.”
Other UAP whistleblowers have faced similar issues after coming forward, from break-ins at their homes to leaked personal details.
The new waiver also only covers those who have worked with the Pentagon, leaving a CIA-sized hole in it.
“I'm glad that they're waiving NDAs for everybody who was on the [Defense Department] side,” Borland says. “It doesn't change the [Intelligence Community] side.”
He pointed to the need to offer similar protections to the alphabet soup of intelligence agencies beyond just the CIA, including the National Security Agency, FBI, and others, as well as science agencies like NASA.
Marik von Rennenkampff, a former State Department analyst and Obama-era Pentagon appointee now at the Sol Foundation, a UAP research nonprofit, agrees with that sentiment because of where whistleblowers say the secrets about nonhuman technology are kept. He points to a specific unit in the CIA that’s “allegedly—allegedly, allegedly, allegedly, I can't stress that enough—the quarterback for this alleged legacy effort.”
“What has been announced publicly does not cover the core of the alleged legacy program yet,” von Rennenkampff tells WIRED.
There's a second gap that no memo can close. Many of the people alleged to hold this information work for private contractors, and the government can't waive an NDA it isn't party to. Only the 2022 statute addresses those types of agreements, and only for disclosures made through the official AARO channel.
Despite these shortcomings, UAP researchers and whistleblowers point to, von Rennenkampff argues this week’s announcement is still important.
“After 80 years of government denial, obfuscation, and ridicule on this topic, there's now true political capital invested in this,” he says. Unlike AARO, PURSUE is a “presidentially directed initiative” that is reporting ultimately to political appointees in the White House, “versus career bureaucrats.”
“It shows that the Trump administration is taking extraordinary claims about retrievals of a craft of nonhuman origins seriously,” he says. There’s a phrase in the release that von Rennenkampff says is another curious detail, particularly given how “wordsmithed to hell” government statements about UAP generally are. The Pentagon wrote that “individuals with direct knowledge of UAP-related programs” have historically feared legal liability for speaking.
“It doesn't say people with partial knowledge, half knowledge, alleging knowledge,” he says. “It says people with direct knowledge.”
Borland's hope is that PURSUE answers to someone with the power to act on what it hears. He points to White House deputy chief of staff for policy Stephen Miller—who Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed is working on the UAP portfolio—as someone who would signal the White House is doing more than paying lip service to the topic.
Beyond that, Borland has an offer.
“There's enough smoke, and there's enough people behind the scenes,” he says, referring to himself and other whistleblowers. “If Stephen Miller and Trump wanted to actually know some stuff, they could call us into the White House right now, and I can throw down, and so can the rest of them.”
results.summary:
The Department of Defense has issued a targeted legal waiver allowing personnel to disclose classified UAP information to a White House-directed program without violating nondisclosure agreements.

### Key Points
- The waiver protects current and former service members, civilian personnel, and contractors from administrative or civil penalties when reporting to the White House-led PURSUE team.
- Protections do not extend to disclosures made to the press, the public, or Congress, and the waiver does not address potential criminal liability under the Espionage Act.
- Critics, including whistleblower Dylan Borland, argue the directive is redundant because existing 2022 legislation already provided similar protections for disclosures made through the Pentagon’s AARO office.
- The policy excludes intelligence agencies like the CIA and the NSA, leaving significant gaps regarding where alleged legacy UAP programs are reportedly housed.
- The initiative signals a shift in political focus, as the White House now directly oversees the collection of information regarding potential nonhuman technology.

### Why it Matters
This directive represents a significant escalation in the government's formal engagement with unidentified anomalous phenomena by bypassing traditional bureaucratic channels in favor of direct White House oversight. While skeptics view the move as limited in scope, it highlights a growing political willingness to investigate long-standing claims of secret, nonhuman technology programs.

results.title: Poland lost $230m in cryptocurrency trying to buy Venezuelan oil in 2023 — USB drives with crypto handed directly to scammers
results.author: editors@tomshardware.com (Bruno Ferreira) , Bruno Ferreira
results.content:
The country of Venezuela has had a few embattled decades, but it has massive oil reserves continually attracting buyers, despite the U.S.-led sanctions that effectively block dealings with the nation. A few years back, in 2023, Poland's state-backed Orlen energy group had $600m in hand and was looking to buy 6 million barrels during a sanction reprieve. Like many before him, one executive thought it expedient to use the USDT stablecoin cryptocurrency (1 USD = 1 USDT). It didn't end well, with $230 million worth of crypto unaccounted for at multiple stages in an adventure chronicled by the Financial Times.
The twisted web of transactions
Orleen enlisted an external company, Hannon, to take care of the purchase, which it did by enlisting the services of UK firm Lexcor Energy, which supposedly had a Venezuelan office. Hannon first needed to convert a large sum into USDT, and did so by exchanging $245m at multiple Dubai companies, adding $15m of its own to the deal. Only one of multiple transfers of $80m into 80m USDT was fully successful.
As for the other two, $135m exchange only produced 85m USDT out the other end, with $50m still unaccounted for. A third exchange of $30m also vanished (partially returning much later). The proverbial PNL is currently -$80m, and Hannon has 165m USDT in hand. All this while, three Polish oil tankers headed to Venezuela anchored there, continually racking up millions in demurrage and port fees, as they were being chartered for far longer than initially agreed.
Weeks of delays followed, which Hannon pinned on Venezuelan energy company PDVSA. One of Hannon's reps, Kam Tse, headed to Venezuela himself with a colleague, loaded with the USDT, stored in multiple cold wallets on USB sticks. They stayed in high-end hotels, drove around in armored cars, and employed bodyguards out of concern for the money and themselves. Tse found many brokers claiming to be from PDVSA, a cadre later revealed to contain a substantial number of con-men, many of whom fled as a local investigation came cracking down.
The buyers were nevertheless undeterred, and they handed 60m USDT in a USB wallet to a purported representative of local energy corp Synergy. After a few weeks of waiting, a Venezuelan office sent him a picture of a purported PDVSA export schedule displaying all three Polish tankers set to be loaded with 1.9m barrels of oil each, but with no predicted date. Ever-trusting, Tse's team then handed Synergy's representative another 50m USDT on another USB wallet. Said representative vanished in a cloud of smoke. PNL currently sits at -$190m.
Seemingly desperate, Tse ordered a buy of 1 million barrels of a lighter blend of oil, eventually finding it contaminated, then switched tactics to acquiring fuel oil instead, signing a contract. At last, a break: some of the money spent in the Dubai exchanges came back; only 21m USDT out of a $30m input, but still better than zero. Tse pays Consulting Services, another Venezuelan firm, 11m USDT for the fuel.
Finally, some good news: 500,000 barrels confirmed loaded onto the one ship, half of the contracted amount. Tse provides Consulting Services with another 11m USDT for the rest of the fuel, but that was never delivered, and there was no further contact. Cumulative PNL = -$186m total. With $72m in shipping costs in total (far outweighing the expected profit), plus additional expenses, the Polish government's investigation pins the total lost and spent at $424m.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
The aftermath
Many folks' gut reaction may be that the use of cryptocurrency made the cash untraceable, but the problem isn't with the blockchain. In fact, for the vast majority of currencies, the on-chain ledger offers more visibility into transactions, not less. What failed here was the lack of official records linking wallets to persons or entities.
Reputable exchanges all have a form of identity verification, known as KYC, mandated by law. The problem is that apparently almost no entities Hannon traded with had any recognizable proof their crypto wallets belonged to them. The Venezuelan crude oil salesmen vanished, effectively cutting off nearly every avenue for investigation. Before their exchanges, they had even advised Tse to not keep records of their transactions due to the government's investigation into their collective's dealings.
Even in Dubai, pending court cases regarding the dollar-to-USDT exchanges hinge on the same problem, despite the presence of verifiable bank transactions. Broadly speaking, the country's legal system places the burden of proof fully on the accuser, making them prove wallet ownership before discussing the meat of the dispute. That's quite the high bar to clear for Hannon in order to prove that it wasn't handed the funds from the exchanges.
That task may well prove impossible, since one can't prove a negative when there's nothing linking the exchange to their wallet. Adding insult to injury, the two exchanges in the court were both recently created, and probably weren't a part of Dubai's VARA program for legal crypto operations. Caveat emptor.

He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.
